newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium agrees 10 billion franc budget review.
newsitem.headline: Belgium agrees 10 billion franc budget review.

text.p: The Belgian government has reached agreement on a 10 billion franc ($286 million) austerity package aimed at keeping the 1997 deficit on target to hit 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), a government spokesman said on Monday.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene will present the budget review, along with a series of measures to boost employment, to parliament on Tuesday at 1500 GMT.
"This is the definitive package. The budget review operation is finished," a budget ministry spokesman said.
In order to qualify for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) Belgium must bring down its fiscal deficit to three percent of GDP from 3.4 percent 1996.
But because Belgium's debt, at 130.6 percent of GDP, is the highest in Europe the country and way above the target for EMU, the country has decided to make an extra effort on the deficit front.

Every spring the Belgian government reviews the budget drafted the previous autumn to make sure it stays on target. Disappointing tax receipts and an overshoot in health spending this year has forced the government to take corrective measures.
Most of the planned measures were leaked to Belgian media on Saturday, but the budget spokesman confirmed that none of the measures would hit consumer spending.
"As (Belgian Budget Minister Herman Van Rompuy) said, this will be a painless budget," he said.
Two of the measures will hit Belgium's corporate world.
A tax on the turnover of pharmaceutical companies will be increased to four percent from one percent, raising 1.8 billion francs in 1997.

Belgian utility company Electrabel NV , which has a virtual monopoly on electricity production in Belgium, will see the tax on its profits rise to 14 percent from 12 percent, raising 1.5 billion francs in 1997.
Electrabel said earlier this month that 1996 group net profit rose to 30.4 billion francs, from 28.8 billion in 1995.

Companies will also be hit by the obligation for non-managing partners in private companies to start paying withholding taxes on their income, which will no longer be seen as a profit, but as a salary. That measure will raise 1.2 billion francs this year.
A crackdown on evasion of value added taxes is expected to bring in an extra two billion francs, while spending cuts side wil save a total of three billion francs.

Defence will contribute 600 million francs, while the Development Cooperation Ministry will see its budget cut by 200 million. An unused 400 million franc budget for third world aid will also be taken back.

Dehaene's centre-left coalition also agreed on a series of measures to boost employment, including the possibility for large companies to cut the working week for staff to 32 hours from 38 hours with reduced wages.

The 32-hour week can be applied only in companies employing more than 50 people, and on condition that employers and workers agree on this at their works council and that the employer's total wage costs do not increase.

Another measure is that people who have been unemployed for more than five years can keep their unemployment benefits if they are hired for service jobs. In that case, the employer will only pay a small extra sum on top of the benefits. ($ = 34.91 Belgian Francs)
